description: The Mool Mantra (GGS 1a), Ik Onkar, and God as Creator — both present within and separate from creation.
content_html:
Sikhism: A Living Tradition

Sikhism is one of the world’s youngest major religions, founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late fifteenth century. It is important to understand from the outset that Sikhism is a distinct, independent religion — not a synthesis of Hinduism and Islam, even though it emerged in a region where both traditions were present. Guru Nanak received what Sikhs believe was a direct revelation from God, and the teachings he proclaimed stand on their own foundations. Today there are approximately 430,000 Sikhs living in Britain, with large communities in Southall (west London), Birmingham, Leicester and Bradford.

The Mool Mantra: The Foundation of Sikh Belief

At the very opening of the Guru Granth Sahib (GGS 1a) stands the Mool Mantra (also spelled Mul Mantar). The phrase “Mool Mantra” means “root formula” or “foundational verse.” It is the first composition in the Guru Granth Sahib and is considered by Sikhs to be the most complete summary of their belief in God. The Mool Mantra opens with the numeral 1 — in Punjabi script, Ik Onkar — followed by a series of attributes.

The Mool Mantra teaches that God is: one (Ik Onkar); the Truth (Sat Nam — whose name is truth); the Creator (Karta Purakh); without fear (Nirbhau); without enmity (Nirvair); beyond time and death (Akal Murat); self-existent (Ajooni Saibhang); and known through the grace of the Guru (Gur Prasad). These attributes paint a picture of God as both utterly transcendent — beyond human comprehension — and intimately present within creation.

Key Fact

The Mool Mantra (GGS 1a) opens with Ik Onkar — “There is one God.” This single statement of absolute monotheism is the cornerstone of all Sikh belief. It is displayed in gurdwaras across Britain and is often the first Punjabi phrase a Sikh child learns.

God as Creator

Sikh teaching holds that God is Karta Purakh — the “Doer,” the Creator being. The universe exists because of God’s hukam (divine will or command). This concept of God as Creator has two dimensions that students must be able to distinguish: God shown in and through the universe, and God as separate from the universe.

First, Sikh teaching holds that God’s presence is visible within creation. The natural world — its beauty, its order, its interdependence — reflects and reveals the divine. Looking at a sunrise over the River Beas near Amritsar, or the community gathered at the Golden Temple, a Sikh sees not just the physical world but a manifestation of divine glory. In this sense God is immanent — permeating all things.

Second, Sikh teaching is clear that God is not identical to the created world. God existed before creation and will exist after it ends. God is not limited by time or physical form. In this sense God is transcendent — entirely other than and beyond the universe. The Mool Mantra’s phrase Akal Murat (deathless form) captures this: God is beyond the cycle of birth, death and decay that governs all created things.

Some students assume that a God who is transcendent (beyond creation) cannot also be immanent (present within creation). Sikh teaching holds both simultaneously. God’s light (jot) is present in every living being, so in that sense God is intimately close. Yet God is also beyond all names, forms and descriptions. The Guru Granth Sahib describes God as nirguna (without attributes — beyond description) and saguna (with attributes — known through creation and the Gurus). This dual nature is not a contradiction for Sikhs; it reflects the vastness of the divine that cannot be confined to any single description.

This matters for the exam. A common student error is to write that “Sikhs believe God IS the universe” (pantheism) or that “God is completely separate and distant.” Neither is accurate. Sikh teaching is that God is present throughout creation (immanent) AND separate from and greater than creation (transcendent).

Ik Onkar and Strict Monotheism

The numeral “1” at the start of the Mool Mantra is not accidental. Guru Nanak’s first public declaration, recorded in the Janamsakhis, was “Na koi Hindu, na koi Musalman” — “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” This was a proclamation that divisions of religion, caste and status do not exist before God. The oneness of God (Ik Onkar) leads directly to the oneness of humanity. Because there is one God, all people share the same divine light within them.

Sikh monotheism is strict. There are no lesser gods or goddesses, no trinity of divine persons, and no deity who is God’s equal or rival. God is addressed in the Guru Granth Sahib by many names — Waheguru (Wondrous Lord), Hari, Ram, Allah — but these are understood as different names for the one, same God. The use of diverse names reflects Guru Nanak’s vision that all humanity, of different faiths and backgrounds, is reaching for the same ultimate reality.

Waheguru is the name most commonly used by Sikhs when speaking of or addressing God. Literally meaning “Wondrous Lord” or “Wonderful Guru,” it captures the sense of awe at God’s greatness. At the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall — the largest gurdwara in Europe — the congregational greeting is Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh (“The Khalsa belongs to the Wondrous Lord; victory belongs to the Wondrous Lord”). This salutation embodies Sikh belief that all belongs to God.

Key Fact

The Mool Mantra describes God as Nirbhau (without fear) and Nirvair (without enmity). These two attributes are linked: because God has no enemies and no fears, God’s love for all creation is completely unconditional. This underpins the Sikh teaching of equality — God’s love is not withheld from any person on the grounds of caste, gender or religion.
exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark Explain question about Sikh beliefs about God, always name your source of authority: the Mool Mantra (GGS 1a). The mark scheme requires reference to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching — without naming the Mool Mantra and at least one attribute from it (e.g. Ik Onkar, Karta Purakh), your response cannot reach the top band. Write two developed reasons: for example, (1) God as Creator — Karta Purakh — with a sentence explaining what this means and why it matters to Sikhs; (2) God as one — Ik Onkar — with a sentence on how this shapes Sikh views of humanity. Each reason needs a “because” or “this means that” to reach the development marks.

For the 12-mark Evaluate question on whether the Mool Mantra is the most important source of Sikh teaching, remember to argue both sides: FOR (it is the opening of the GGS, it is the first prayer children learn, it summarises all belief); AGAINST (the Guru Granth Sahib as a whole is equally important, the lives of the Gurus show belief in action). Always end with a justified conclusion — state which side you find stronger and why. Without a conclusion, the answer cannot reach the highest band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Mool Mantra (GGS 1a) is the foundational statement of Sikh belief, opening with Ik Onkar — “There is one God” — and describing God as Creator, Truth, fearless, without enmity and beyond time.
  • Sikhs understand God as both immanent (present within creation, with divine light in every being) and transcendent (beyond and greater than creation, not limited to physical form).
  • Sikh monotheism is strict and distinct — not a blend of other religions. God’s oneness (Ik Onkar) leads directly to the equality of all humanity, a central teaching of Guru Nanak.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct translation of 'Ik Onkar'?
A) There is one community
B) There is one God
C) God is within us
D) God is the Guru
practice_questions.marks: B) There is one God [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the scripture in which the Mool Mantra is found.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Guru Granth Sahib (accept GGS or Guru Granth Sahib Ji).

practice_questions.text: State two attributes of God as expressed in the Mool Mantra.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: one God (Ik Onkar); the Truth (Sat Nam); the Creator (Karta Purakh); without fear (Nirbhau); without enmity (Nirvair); beyond time/deathless (Akal Murat); self-existent (Ajooni Saibhang); known through the Guru's grace (Gur Prasad).

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting beliefs about the nature of God in Sikhism.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Students may include:
- God as immanent: God's light (jot) is present within creation and within every living being — this means Sikhs see the divine in all people and in the natural world (1 mark identification, 1 mark development).
- God as transcendent: God is beyond and separate from creation, not limited by time or form — the Mool Mantra phrase Akal Murat (deathless form) shows God is beyond the cycle of birth and death that governs all created things (1 mark identification, 1 mark development).
Do not accept answers that imply Sikhism is pantheist (God equals the universe) or that God is wholly remote and unknowable.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Mool Mantra is important to Sikhs.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two well-developed reasons, each with a link to the Mool Mantra (GGS 1a) or another Sikh source. Reasons clearly explained with 'because' or 'this means that' reasoning. Possible points: (1) It is the foundational statement of all Sikh belief — opening the Guru Granth Sahib as GGS 1a, it is the first teaching a child encounters and the basis for all Sikh theology; the attribute Ik Onkar encapsulates strict monotheism. (2) It shapes Sikh ethics — because God is Nirvair (without enmity), Sikhs are called to treat all people as equally loved by God, underpinning sewa and equality.
Secure (3-4 marks): Reasons present and mostly accurate; source named but not fully developed.
Developing (1-2 marks): One reason stated with limited development; source absent or inaccurate.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant knowledge shown.

practice_questions.text:
'The Mool Mantra is the most important source of Sikh teaching about God.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
- refer to Sikh teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The Mool Mantra opens the Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 1a, giving it primacy of place among all Sikh scriptures.
- It is the most concise and complete statement of Sikh belief — describing God as one, the Creator, beyond fear and enmity, and beyond time in a single short passage.
- It is the first prayer many Sikh children learn, making it foundational to Sikh identity and spiritual formation.
- Amritdhari Sikhs recite it in the Nitnem (daily prayers), emphasising its centrality in living Sikh practice.

Arguments against:
- The Guru Granth Sahib as a whole is the eternal Guru — the entire scripture, not just the Mool Mantra, is the living word of God for Sikhs. The 1,430 pages of the GGS contain vast teaching that goes far beyond the Mool Mantra.
- The Janamsakhis (narratives of Guru Nanak's life) and the Dasam Granth provide additional sources of understanding God's nature.
- Lived sewa and sangat (community) may be seen as equally important ways of knowing and responding to God.
- Some Sikhs would argue that Waheguru is known through experience of God — through nam japna (meditating on God's name) — more than through any single text.

Mastering (10-12 marks): Both sides argued with religious sources named; justified conclusion reached, explaining which side is stronger and why.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, generally accurate; conclusion reached but not fully justified.
Developing (4-6 marks): Mostly one-sided; some religious knowledge; limited conclusion.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, little or no source reference, no conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: The Mool Mantra is found at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib at reference ___.
The Sikh attribute 'Nirbhau' means God is without _____.
Sikhs believe God is both _____ (present within creation) and transcendent (beyond and above creation).
Match each Punjabi term from the Mool Mantra to its meaning:

flashcard_questions.a: The foundational Sikh statement of belief, opening the Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 1a.
There is one God — the first words of the Mool Mantra, asserting strict Sikh monotheism.
The Creator — God as the being who brought the universe into existence by divine will.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Nirbhau' mean in the Mool Mantra?
flashcard_questions.a: Without fear — God has no fear of any power or force in existence.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Nirvair' mean in the Mool Mantra?
flashcard_questions.a: Without enmity — God holds no hostility towards any part of creation.
Deathless form — God is beyond time and the cycle of birth and death.
The divine will or command of God by which the universe was created and is governed.

flashcard_questions.q: What does it mean to say God is 'immanent' in Sikhism?
flashcard_questions.a: God's light (jot) is present within creation and within every living being.

flashcard_questions.q: What does it mean to say God is 'transcendent' in Sikhism?
flashcard_questions.a: God is beyond and separate from creation — not limited by time, form or physical existence.
The most widely used Sikh name for God, meaning Wondrous Lord, expressing awe and devotion.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Sikhism described as a distinct religion, not a synthesis of Hinduism and Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: Guru Nanak received a direct revelation from God — Sikh teachings stand on their own foundations.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Guru Granth Sahib?
flashcard_questions.a: The eternal living scripture of Sikhism, regarded as the eleventh and final Guru.

glossary_terms.definition: The foundational statement of Sikh belief, opening the Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 1a, summarising the nature of God.
The opening phrase of the Mool Mantra, meaning 'There is one God' — the basis of Sikh monotheism.
The eternal living scripture of Sikhism, regarded as the eleventh and final Guru, containing the hymns of the ten human Gurus.
An attribute of God from the Mool Mantra meaning 'the Creator' — God who brought the universe into existence.
The divine will or command of God; the order by which God created and continues to govern the universe.
The most widely used Sikh name for God, meaning 'Wondrous Lord', expressing devotion and wonder at the divine.
In Sikh belief, God's presence throughout creation — God's light (jot) is found within every living being.
In Sikh belief, God as beyond and above creation — not limited to or identified with the physical universe.
